utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence and that still applies. Now, I think Ms. Zivkovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, good afternoon. My name is Jasmina Zivkovic and together with my learned colleague Antonio Apostolski I appear for Mr. Johan Tarculovski. Mr. Rexhepi, from your statement we see that you served a conscription military service. Can you tell us which branch of the military service you were serving in.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any training in handling infantry weapons while you were in the army?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such training. No. From the very first day I was a driver. I don't know how to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told my learned colleagues from the Prosecution and from the Defence that the shelling and the shooting against the village of Ljuboten started early in the morning on the Friday, the 10th of August, and you stated that the shooting came from the mountains up north from the direction of Brace's house and from the direction of the church. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw it all from your house.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen them from the house when they were shooting from the direction of the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Which means that you didn't see any shooting coming from the direction of the Brace's house and from the mountains, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were hidden in the basement. If we go to the balcony you could see them from the mountain as well. But from the Brace's house, it's far away. It can be seen very well. And this is where the check-point was, the police check-point was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: But considering the distance, you couldn't see who was shooting exactly.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was shooting. No one else could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you couldn't see that from the distance where you were at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shootings were coming from that side, and that side was entirely under the control of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You also told my colleague Residovic, confirmed that you knew that the army was not shooting from the direction of the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told my colleague Residovic that you knew that the army was not shooting from the direction of the church. And in your statement you also stated that you knew that the person was not a soldier, considering that the army was outside the village. Can we agree with this?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please state the question more clearly and shortly. Don't make such long questions. I don't understand them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the army was not shooting from the direction of the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which army? The police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Macedonian army.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was shooting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And also when my colleague asked you you stated categorically that the NLA was not responsible for the mine that killed the Macedonian soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, please. Repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, my colleague asked you whether you knew something about the tragedy when the mine was planted at Ljubotenski Bacila, and you stated that you knew that the NLA had not been responsible for that attack. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mine was put very far from the village. I don't know, but it's not possible for the NLA to have put the mine there. It was under the police control. The mine was put near to a police check-point. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also stated that you knew that the terrorists were not inside the village of Ljuboten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no NLA in Ljuboten village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has also asked you, did you know that many people left the village as early as on the Friday, and you told her that you didn't know, since Ljuboten is a large village. How would you know then that there were no terrorists there?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were NLA soldiers, I believe that Macedonians would not have been able to enter there to do massacres, to burn houses to kill children, and so on. It wouldn't have entered the village as it didn't enter any other village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you must have heard about the frequent attacks of the terrorists to the neighbouring villages, which took place before this event in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a brief objection. My learned colleague is assuming that the NLA are terrorists and I think that within this question it should be distinguished if she's talking about the NLA or if she's talking about another organisation, terrorist organisation. But she is defining the NLA as a terrorist group within her question. And that is the third time it has occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That does seem to be a disputed issue in this trial Ms. Zivkovic. So I think you need to decide whether you're asking about the NLA or whether you're asking about terrorists and they may be quite different in the minds of many speakers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will reframe my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, do you know, have you heard about the frequent attacks by the NLA on the neighbouring villages, attacks that happened before this event in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What attack? There were no NLA attacks in our village. The other villages are far away. You know that our village is surrounded by Macedonian villages. It is the only Albanian village there. I cannot speak of other villages. I can only speak of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that the police stationed its check-point there and that the army was deployed at those positions precisely because of the attacks?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did that only with the civilians, with villagers that have day and night worked in their fields. The police knew perfectly hat there was no NLA in Ljuboten. They are one million per cent sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you surely knew that the NLA was in the mountains, above Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was in the mountains over Ljuboten. I don't know how much you understand where Ljuboten is located. Two to three months Ljuboten was surrounded by police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at the check-point Kodra e Zajmit together with your brother and your father?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you surely remember that your father tried to make the police officer let your brother you yourself go free; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this, because my father was taken and let down on the ground. When the children started crying, he then stood up and went with the children and he was -- the police let him go at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement you said that on Friday afternoon a shell fell at about 10, 15 metres from you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: On Friday afternoon, if I understood well, you were first in the house of Avdil Ali and then you stayed there for several hours and then you returned to your own home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the bomb -- the grenade explode, and when -- after the grenade exploded I went there in the basement. The grenade that killed this child six or five-year-old year's child.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer my question. My question was whether you went to the house of Avdil Ali first.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the grenade exploded I went there and I hid myself in the basement. I flee from the grenade. I laid down on the ground when it exploded and then I crawled until the house of Avdil, 30 metres away from the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you stayed there for several hours and then you stayed at your home -- you returned to your home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And upon your return home with the other members of your family, you went to the basement, where you stayed until Sunday, 12th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And on Sunday, you joined several other Ljuboten villagers in the basement of Reshat Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Reshat Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Reshat, I apologise. None of the persons in the basement had any weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, considering the situation calmed down, you decided to leave the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You were told that someone would come to pick you up, someone from the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we arrived on the field of the village, we walked by the river. No one told us if there were foreigners, internationals there. It was just our opinion and our idea to leave the village. To leave the village in order to stay alive. No one knew that someone would come to pick us up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what time it was when you started from the village? Roughly, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. It was after 12.00. I cannot give the exact hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were leaving the village, you didn't see any car belonging to any of the international organisations in the village or down the road you were walking.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't see any. We were trying to leave the village hiding, because people -- they were shooting from the -- from the side of the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You actually, if I understood you well, were among the last ones to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a small group behind us. I was with a larger group before. I think there were people that left after us. I'm not sure. I just can tell of myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And from this check-point, Kodra e Zajmit, you were first transferred to the Butel police station, then to Karpos police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that my learned colleague from the Prosecution office showed you a document, an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 149.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this Official Note in front of you?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you can also see your name?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are these the persons listed here -- were the persons listed here with you?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In prison they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an Official Note of the Cair police station?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that the -- from the police -- Butel police station we were given any documents. I don't remember this. I can tell you about the people who were in prison for whom I read in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the names that are listed here? Were those the people that were with you together in the police station or in the cell? Of course, if you could remember.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see even myself in that cell. I was not conscious. I couldn't see anyone or I couldn't know anyone there. We were beaten up there. I had a lot of pain. I couldn't recognise people -- the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning that you don't know whether those persons were interviewed or not; is that correct? That is, in the police station of Karpos.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all interviewed, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that were all subjected to the paraffin glove test?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were subjected to this test. I didn't know whether I myself was subjected to this test, but it -- but I tested positive. The police did whatever it wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you surely know that -- do you know that this is the test which determines whether fire-arms were used or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the paraffin glove test is a test which determines the use of fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one who touched any weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Please respond to my question. Do you know that this is the test that determines the use of fire-arms or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Also when my learned colleague from the Prosecutor's office showed you the same document, she asked you whether in the police station of Karpos you were interviewed, and you responded to that that you weren't. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which police station are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The police station where this Official Note comes from that you can see on the screen, Karpos police station.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when we were subjected to the paraffin test, this was the only contact. We were not interrogated. We were only beaten up. For 72 hours we were beaten up with everything they had in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown his statement, 65 ter 2D00179, 2D02-0964, of 4th of October, 2004, page 6, paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: In the second line of paragraph 30 of your statement you say the following: "[In English] There were some 10 to 15 other people in that office when I enter it. I remember that one of them was a female police officer, and some men were wearing civilian clothes. I take it they were some inspector, since they were discussing some professional issues with one who interviewed me. The men in green T shirt was reading some document that was accusing of me having been fighting in the NLA and that I had thrown my uniform somewhere and that I had been armed and that I had given myself up to the police but I told him that was not true." [Interpretation] From this statement of yours, it seems that you were nevertheless interviewed.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at the time when we were subjected to the paraffin test. I think this was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you did discuss with some police officer.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't speak anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, I just read out what you said. My question was whether what you have stated in your statement is the truth.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were taken before the court on Tuesday, and as far as I could understand, you refused to have a lawyer, but one was assigned to you ex officio?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you were taken to the Sutka prison, where you physically attacked a guard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have beat him if I could, but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But during your stay in the prison, nobody beated you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even the doctor beat me. The doctor I went to see because I had a headache. He kicked me in the stomach and he said, You'll have nothing, then we have been mistreated in the prison as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask again for the witness to be shown his statement, 65 ter 2D00179 -- oh, that it is already displayed on the screen. We only need to see page 7, paragraph 34. No, I apologise. Page 7, paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence of this paragraph you say: "[In English] 125 days, during this time, there were no beatings anymore. We also got food and water and were treated almost like the normal prisoners, although the guards used to call us terrorists and our conditions were a bit stricter that they were for the normal prisoners." [Interpretation] Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After two months's time in prison, they started to different acting, this was the case. They acted as the weather changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And then there was a procedure against you before the Skopje Basic Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you stated before this Court on the Friday, since you did not have a lawyer, my colleague showed you the power of attorney of your wife, but you claimed that you were not able to even report what happened to you because you did not have a lawyer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Could you please repeat the question once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I will make this question a bit simpler. Do you remember saying that during the procedure that was carried out against you, you had no lawyer?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we appeared before the court, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and during the procedure while you were in prison.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a lawyer. I told to the other person also that there was a person that came to see me. He didn't show me any document. He only asked me a few questions about my health and that's all. I didn't have any lawyer. I didn't take any lawyer. Maybe the others took a lawyer, but I was not shown any document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the document 65 ter 2D00332.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, do you see this document displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation that you're able to see here is the working version, because we didn't have these documents translated into English. And that is part of the Exhibit P50.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, do you know Enver Rexhepikovski?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is he your brother?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that he gave the power of attorney to the attorney Dragan Vasilevski, whereby your name is precisely mentioned. On 14th of August, 2001, he was authorised to represent you? I apologise, that is August 20.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you are making the question to me whether I took a lawyer. You are not asking my brother. I didn't take myself a lawyer. You are asking me and not my brother. What was being done outside, I don't know. I was in the prison. And the person that came to see me, he didn't say he was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, but you claim that you had not -- that have you no attorney at all.

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't have. He didn't say he was a lawyer. I don't know who was that person that came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown -- I apologise. Your Honours, could this be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D33, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask now that the witness is shown the document 65 ter 2D00331. Your Honours, this is also a working version of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, do you see this document displayed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that this is a motion of the same lawyer, whereby he informs the court for being your attorney, received on 22nd of August, 2001, by the Basic Court Skopje II?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask -- I would seek to tender this document in evidence as well. That is also part of Exhibit P50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to show the witness document ERN number 0643. That is also P47 ERN number 0463-8891-029, and the English version is 0463-8919-01.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, you said that your lawyer only came to see you, but in front of you -- well, I don't know if you could see it or not, whether you could see the Macedonian version. This is a decision whereby the court rejects the appeal of your attorney. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Zivkovic. Ms. Regue, are there questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, good afternoon. I would ask to you listen carefully to my questions before answering. On Sunday, the 12th of August, before your house was set on fire, did you see or hear any shell falling on your house?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the house was burned? Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Before your house was set on fire, did you see or hear any shell falling on your house, before, right before?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You were also asked about the house of Harun Rexhepi, your neighbour. You testified that you found out that his house was burned when you were in Sutka. Were you told which day the house was burned?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three houses were burned on that same day, but I learned about his house later, while I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And which is that same day? Could you state the date, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Sunday, 12th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: My learned colleague also showed to you the paraffin test that-- with a positive result. Did you ever hold any weapon during the weekend 10 to 12 August 2001?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, did you consider the NLA a terrorist organisation in 2001?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You were also asked that in Sutka prison you tried to attack a guard. You answer that you would have beat him if you could. Why you couldn't beat him, Mr. Rexhepi?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was beaten and he was cursing me. He was calling me a terrorist. He was saying that, You should be killed, you should be murdered.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honours, could I please have display Exhibit P00050, pages 45 to 54. And if we can go to the first page of both versions. The next page. Sorry, the page before this one N002-2128. The page before this one, please. Thanks. If we could have an English version. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Rexhepi, you have been questioned about the procedures against you. This is the indictment dated as we see in the upper left side 7th September, 2001 from the Basic Public Prosecution to Skopje Court II. We see indictment as a title and we see your name in the second paragraph. If we could move now to the fifth page in both versions, English and Macedonian, please. The English version, I think, doesn't correspond with the ... The ERN should be N002-0132. 0132. Mr. Rexhepi, I'm going to read to you the charges pressed against you. It says in the middle paragraph: "On 12 August 2001, between 8.00 and 12.00 in the village of Ljuboten," they, meaning you and your fellow villagers, "participated in an armed conflict as combatants against the Republic of Macedonia, in such a way that during the intensive combatting actions, acted against the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia. Located near the village with infantry fire-arms and ammunition. Up until the moment when they were forced to withdraw disposing of the equipments and equipment that they had while withdrawing." Mr. Rexhepi, on 12 August 2001 between 8.00 and 12.00 hours did you participate in an armed conflict against the Macedonian forces?

utterances.speaker: QAMURAN REXHEPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were in the basement. We were there. Nobody took part in such a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Regue. You'll be pleased to know, sir, that concludes the questioning there is. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give. The court officer will now show you out, and you may of course return now to your home and your ordinary activities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Simply to indicate that we would wish to make a number of short submissions at the end of the day in relation to three related matters, Your Honour, but we believe there is one that should be raised in private session prior to the next witness being brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe there may also be some from Mr. Saxon. Is that right, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think start with Mr. Saxon and move to you then Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, the Prosecution would like to -- excuse me, the Prosecution would like to correct a mistake, which it made when it sent its most recent witness schedule to the Chamber and the parties. The next witness, Mr. Risto Galevski, has an estimated time of three hours. That is incorrect. According to the Prosecution's recent submission, that should be three days or 11.25 hours, Your Honour. Before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And of that time how long does the Prosecution anticipate spending in its evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two hours and 30 minutes, Your Honour. Two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness arrives, the Prosecution would like to raise a matter regarding him and perhaps we could move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as I have indicated we will consider those submissions over the break. Now, Mr. Mettraux, you have other matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, thank you. The first one relates to the picture of the diseased Mr. Rami Jusufi. It is a picture Rule 65 ter 608 which was used both by the Defence and by the Office of the Prosecutor with Witness 171 and by the Defence with Dr. Jakovski. We had failed at the time to tender this document formally. We would wish to do at this stage. The Prosecution has no objection, Your Honour, and I could give the ERN for the record. It is 0501-626 and it is Rule 65 ter 608. It's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. The other matter, Your Honour, which we would like to respond at this stage is the Prosecution third proposed amended witness list. It is a motion to withdraw I believe 13 witnesses from its list and the application was made on the 12th of July of 2007. The Defence would wish to indicate at this stage that we will have no objection to the withdrawal of all 13 witnesses concerned by this application. There are three matters, however, which we would wish to place on the transcript at this stage on the record. The first one is that it is the Defence understanding that the Prosecution will not seek or at least not be permitted to seek to rely on the statements or the evidence of the witnesses which they now seek to withdraw from this its list. The second matter which we like to place on the record at this stage is that the application of the Prosecution in relation to the withdrawal of these witnesses may in fact impact on the admissibility of a number of documents, some of which may have been directly or indirectly related to a particular witness and that the consideration in relation to admissibility of evidence has been factored in by the Prosecution in its application. The last and third matter which we would like to record at this stage is that it is our understanding that the Prosecution will not be permitted later on in its case to seek from the Trial Chamber to draw certain inferences on particular facts when the witnesses or some of the witnesses which are now being withdrawn were the most appropriate to give positive evidence in relation to these facts. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in respect to the withdrawal of the witnesses by the Prosecution, I completely support the position of my colleague, Mr. Mettraux, and I am at his side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to respond on my feet to the rather broad understandings that my colleague has just expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought they were the product of discussion between you. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But let me try. The Prosecution -- with regard to Mr. Mettraux's first point, that Mr. Mettraux is making his submission not to object to the withdrawal of these 13 witnesses based on the understanding that the Prosecution will not seek to rely on the evidence of any of these witnesses or their statements. The Prosecution cannot make that affirmation at this time, because at a minimum, if there is a Defence case during this trial, the Prosecution might seek to use one or more witness statements during cross-examination of a Defence witness. So the Prosecution cannot affirm the first point that my colleague raised. With respect to the second point, whether -- and perhaps I didn't understand it clearly, whether the Prosecution has factored in whether these particular 13 witnesses would be the best person -- would be the best witnesses with respect to the admissibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the third or the second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe it is the second point, Your Honour. I could be wrong. Whether the Prosecution has factored in, whether evidence that may be tendered in the future would have been appropriately tendered through one of these 13 witnesses, again, the -- it's difficult for the prosecution give a blankets affirmation of what it has factored in into its thinking. However, I will say this. The Prosecution's position is if in the future it has evidence which it feels it should and can tender, it will seek to do it through an appropriate witness or from a motion at the bar table. Whether evidence is tendered through what is termed the most appropriate witness is a difficult calculation for the Prosecution to make at this time, given the complexity of this trial and the complexity of the evidence. There was a third point as to whether the Prosecution would not draw any inferences from the evidence or the statements given by witnesses whom the Prosecution now proposes be dropped from its list. Quite frankly, the Prosecution doesn't understand this question. We're not quite sure which kinds of inferences my colleague is referring to. Certainly if there are inferences that can be drawn appropriately from evidence that is to come in this case, the Prosecution may attempt to do so, whether they are related to witnesses who have been dropped or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honour, to indicate that we had given the indication on Friday already, on Thursday or Friday of last week that the matter would be raised. It wasn't possible on Friday to do so, so we have done it today. Concerning the last issue and the issue of inferences, this is inferences which the Prosecution will seek to draw from the Chamber, not from the evidence which was withdrawn. Concerning the issue of the evidence, Your Honour, there are document or there appears to be document which are on the Prosecution list and which are directly or very intimately, if I may use that term, linked to a particular witness. We do understand that there are situation where a document could be tendered through a second or even a third best witness. There are situation, however, where the fact of withdrawing a particular witness particularly when that witness is the person who prepared the document or otherwise knows about the circumstances in which it was prepared, the Prosecution would have to take into consideration the possibility that this withdrawal would be a factor relevant to the admission or otherwise of the document. As concern the issue of -- the first issue, the reliance on evidence, there is also another matter which in fairness to my colleague Mr. Saxon it is and the point that we are making also was the reliance which other witnesses which the Prosecution intend to call may seek to draw references which these witnesses may want to make to statements or the evidence of witnesses who are being now withdrawn. It is it our understanding that having taken the considered decision to withdraw these witnesses, the Prosecution will not be permitted to rely on this statement through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I clarify one point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With regard to my colleague's point that the withdrawal of a witness or witnesses is a factor to be considered vis-a-vis the admissibility of evidence through another witness, well, the Prosecution disagrees. In the Prosecution's submission, the Trial Chamber needs to make a decision regarding admissibility of evidence pursuant to Rule 89 C. Those are the only criteria that the Prosecution has to -- excuse me -- that the chamber should consider. Prosecution does believe that a number of documents, for example that the Prosecution initially planned to tender through Ali Ahmeti may now be tendered through another witness, but it is the Prosecution's position that as long as that witness who remains on the list can properly authenticate the material and speak to its relevance and probative value, whether another witness has been withdrawn from the list should really not be an element in the calculation regarding admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Not so unusually in this trial, it is it not surprising the Chamber does not agree precisely with the position taken by either party. The motion at the moment is for the withdrawal from its list of potential witnesses of 13 of those witnesses. If that is done, the Prosecution reasonably advances the view that that will assist in the shortening of this trial, a trial at the moment that appears to take -- appears to be expected to take in the Prosecution phase over twice the time that was estimated for the Prosecution case at the beginning of the trial. And that is an estimate if these 13 witnesses are withdrawn. If not, the trial will be even longer. The Chamber is concerned to ensure that the trial is conducted in a shorter time. As is consistent with the fairness and adequacy of the trial. And it certainly will not put time in the way of a fair presentation of the Defence case, which is a matter which we have to keep under observation at all times, even though it means that the length of the trial will stretch out. But, of course, on the other hand, the longer the trial continues, the more that delay is against the interest of each of the accused and against the interest of other accused waiting their turn to be tried. So the Chamber must balance those considerations. With respect to these 13 witnesses, the Chamber will look at the merit of the question, whether there is a reason why they should not be withdrawn from the list. And the primary basis for that would be that to do so would create an unfairness for the accused. In the absence of demonstrated unfairness, if the Prosecution wishes to shorten the extent of the case it presents, either by removing witnesses that are essentially duplicating each or by narrowing some of the allegations that they rely on, that is a matter essentially for the Prosecution's judgement and decision. We are concerned that by doing so there will not be unfairness. In the absence of agreement between the parties, the Chamber would agree with the hesitation of Mr. Saxon about each of the three matters that Mr. Mettraux has put forward. If at the moment there is no sufficient demonstration of a reason why the witness list should not be shortened and the Chamber were to agree to that shortening, the trial will then continue on the basis of the witnesses who are called, and questions of the admissibility of evidence will be determined according to the Rules and the ordinary principles. And the fact that an exhibit might have been tendered through another witness doesn't mean that it will not be admissible if tendered through some other witness, even though the other witness may not be able to say as much about the exhibit as the first. If it is admissible through the other witness, it would normally be expected to be admitted. The same position would be taken by the Chamber with respect to the other two issues raised by Mr. Mettraux. We will have to look at each cause for objection, if there is an objection, about an exhibit or another witness relying on it, or about the use of a statement, according to the ordinary Rules applicable. So. In the absence of agreement between the parties, the Chamber would not be prepared to impose any one of the three types of limitations or conditions advanced by Mr. Mettraux. Now, I think, Mr. Mettraux, that leaves you in this position: Either you must object to the witnesses or some of them being removed to the list; and if so, then advance specifically what you see to be the unfairness to your client from the withdrawal. Unless you satisfy us on those matters, for the reasons indicated, the Chamber is likely to agree to the witnesses being removed from the list. You will probably want to reflect on that a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think we can state our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. Well, please go ahead and state it. I've said those things to make it clear to you that you will have to make decisions yourself at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our position is that, indeed, we will have no objection to the application made by the Prosecution; and if indeed one of the three matters which we stated as a matter of caution for the witnesses and evidence to come, the course which we will take will be to object on an individual basis if and when problems, if any, arise with particular witnesses, as we foresee might arise with one or two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mettraux be kind enough to repeat the ERN number of the tendered page of 65 ter 608, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: With pleasure. That would be 0501-6266, and that would be 1D104. It is it also a Rule 65 ter 608, from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Mettraux. In view of the position indicated by the parties, the Chamber would indicate that it would grant the motion of the Prosecution for the withdrawal of the 13 witnesses that has been proposed. Reasons have been sufficiently indicated in the comments I made a moment ago which were intended essentially to alert Mr. Mettraux to our position. So that motion will be granted. In view of the time, we now must take the first break. We will resume at a quarter past 4.00 to receive the evidence of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, will you call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will call General Risto Galevski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well, we've lost the usher, so ... Your Honours, perhaps while we're waiting for witness, to use the time, we have some binders with some exhibits that we hope to show to the next witness. If Ms. Guduric could provide them to the Chamber and to the Defence, please, and one for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the sheet what is given to you now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Before you commence your evidence, General, could I mention to you a matter about our general procedures, which I would bring to your attention, that is, that as a witness, you may object to answering a question which you believe would incriminate you. The Chamber has no particular reason to think that this issue will arise, but we have only a general knowledge of matters about which you are going to speak and because you were positioned -- still in a position of some seniority in the police force of Macedonia, we think it useful that you be aware of that in case in your own knowledge of your circumstances you see that that difficulty might present itself. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, are you General Risto Galevski?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, are you hearing me in your own language, Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe your current employment, please.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Up until a few days ago, I was state advisor in the cabinet of the Ministry of the Interior. Since the 10th of July, a decision appoints me to the job of assistant to the minister for the sector of European Union. I haven't started working at that position yet, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, the education -- let me go back. What year did you join the Macedonian police?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I am employed in the police of the Republic of Macedonia since 1st of August, 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you start off as a routine police officer?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, a routine police officer, in the patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe the education and training that you've received during your police career.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: After I graduated from the secondary police school in 1975, and after I started working, as I have mentioned already, I enrolled at the faculty for defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Faculty for -- interpreter's correction, faculty for security.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: -- As a part-time student, which would mean that I worked and studied at the same time, I was a student while I was still working, in order to graduate from the faculty for security. Apart from my regular education, I also went to various courses, education activities, seminars, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you receive, for example, police training abroad, outside the Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: The first one was in October 1995, in Sicily in Italy. I remember it better than the others because it was the first time I went abroad in such purpose, in such role. And it was interesting because the topic was protection of privacy when using modern technologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall, General, what your position was in August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I was head of the police department, actually uniformed police department in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall that on the 13th of August, 2001 the minister then, Minister Boskoski, appointed you to be a member of a commission?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I am sure that I was appointed a member of such committee, but I could not recall the date. I could not confirm or deny the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can call up, please, from e-court what is Exhibit P00073. Your Honours, this is tab 1 in your binder. And perhaps with the court usher's assistance we could show him the same document in the binder that is on -- we could show General Galevski the same document that is on his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if General Galevski could turn to the Macedonian version of tab 1. General, this is a document -- it says at the top Republic of Macedonia, Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you see that up at the top?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then below that we see the date, 13 August 2001, and then it says Skopje. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below that we see the words decision to establish a commission. And then part 1 says: "A commission is established to consider the circumstances and analyse the activities under taken by the Special Forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks by terrorist groups on the 12th of August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje." And then it says comprised of Goran Mitevski, director of the bureau for public security, chairman; Risto Galevski, head of the department for police, member; and Zivkovic Petrovski, head of the department for criminal police, member. Now that second member, Risto Galevski, that was you, right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And down in part 2 the decision says,"Based upon data reports and other available materials from the relevant services of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, as well as based upon information obtained in conversation with members of the ministry, the commission for item 1 of the decision has the task to review the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the Security Forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to repel the armed attacks of terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje." Then in part 3, "The commission is obliged immediately to start carrying out the tasks and to prepare a report about the determined facts with an opinion about the grounds, justification and regularity of the activities undertaken by the Security Forces of the ministry." Part 4: "The report from part 3 of this decision shall be submitted to the minister of internal affairs." And then down below we see the signature of Minister Boskoski and the seal of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you recall that this was the decision that made you a member of this commission now?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, so there were three members of this commission, according to this decision. Were all of them members of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you recall, General, how many times the three members of the commission met to discuss the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Six years later, or somewhere around six years, I could not give you a precise answer, although out of the three of us who were members of this committee or task force, the head of the group or the president of that committee, Goran Mitevski is a person I had regular contacts with, although I had less frequent meetings with Mr. Petrovski, I could not state exactly how less regular, due to personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Would it help to you refresh your memory, General, if I showed you the statement that you gave to members of the Office of the Prosecutor in December of 2004? Would that help to you refresh your memory about this point?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Maybe yes, maybe no. I don't know, I don't recall what I have stated then, although I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the assistance the usher, we have copies of this statement. If we could distribute them, please, to the parties and to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe it would be proper for my colleague to ask the question first of the witness, for us to hear what the witness knows and only later, if it is needed, to give the statement to the witness. At this moment, the witness tried to give some reasons and he was interrupted so we do not what the witness actually tried to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, what was said by the witness was sufficient to indicate that he presently claimed not to have a memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe we have copies for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps with the usher's assistance, General Galevski, could you turn to paragraph 6 of that statement. I'd like to review it with you, please. And if we can start at the beginning of that paragraph it says the following: "Being asked how the commission was conducting the investigations, I reply that the commission did not work in the same manner as the commissions normally worked. By this I mean it was mainly Goran Mitevski who conducted the investigations. He then, as far as I remember, kept myself and perhaps Petrovski informed about progress of the investigation. I cannot remember any details, but I remember that Mitevski was very nervous and very upset about the fact that he had to work without any resources and without any real information. However, since I know him, and I know he is a professional officer, I was confident that he was doing his work in a professional manner." And then the last sentence, General, says this: "I remember that the members of the commission never met each other during the investigation." Now, is this -- what is stated in paragraph 6, is this accurate? Does it help you refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I would only like to clarify that the interpretation of the statement is incomplete, since it reads here that I stated Goran Mitevski had mainly been in charge of the investigation and that we did not meet. I don't think I stated anything of the sort, because we met very frequently, but not all three of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to the first page of that statement, General Galevski, the very first page. And if you could look at each page, you see your signature on the bottom of each page, starting from the first page?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I don't see my signature on the translation. Let me look at the original. Yes. It is right, but why has that conclusion been inferred, I can't say. But let me clarify. Probably I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need to clarify something. Have you been following along in the Macedonian translation or in the English, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to you please turn to the Macedonian trans -- I'd like to you please look at the Macedonian translation of your statement so you can follow it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can the usher please assist General Galevski, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I follow the Macedonian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, very well. This is a statement, then, that you signed in 2004. Can we agree that your memory of the events in 2004 would have been fresher than it was today, three years further removed from 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I don't know whether you will understand me properly, but day in, day out, the events come clearer to me and I think I know more than the events now than at three years later, and if you would like to listen, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me stick with the work of the commission for a few minutes, if that's all right. Do you recall, General, how many witnesses or other persons you interviewed during the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I personally did not interview a single one, not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Since when I told you that I could explain why I see the events now more clearly compared to the period immediately after the events--

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, I would like to you answer my questions, all right? Do you recall how many witness statements taken by other commission members were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall if other members of the commission, the other two members, interviewed witnesses, took notes or took statements from them, and showed these notes of their statements to you?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: The committee was not the body conducting the investigation. As far as I understood the task, it was a task force that needed to initiate the mechanisms available to the ministry of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski -- well, I'm going to let you finish that response but then I have another question that I need to put to you. Do you want to add anything more to your last response? You said that the committee was not the body conducting the investigation.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Not literally since neither the director nor the head of the criminal police department nor the police general will allow for the sakes of their positions, the offices that they hold to go down the hierarchy and interview persons who would be interesting for a more serious police or pre-trial investigation. Due to these reasons, the committee headed by the director Goran Mitevski did what it could do. Unfortunately, there was nothing much it could do. This is exactly what I wish to clarify for you, since, as far as I know and as I have studied, in order to start any procedural action after well-based suspicion is established or basic information are obtained and we heard them through verbal information without any report, without any tangible data, one should go on the scene and then inspect the scene of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you ask you a question, General Galevski? You said: "Unfortunately, there was nothing much it could do," there was nothing much the committee could do. Why do you feel that why, or why did you feel that way?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: It couldn't do because we could not go to the scene, not just the three of us. In a system like ours, it is an investigating judge and a public Prosecutor together with an expert team from the forensics police of the ministry of interior going to the scene in order to gather all relevant facts from the actual scene. Unfortunately, it did not happen. It was not possible for it to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I asked you previously, and I need to ask you again, whether any of the other commission members showed you any notes of interviews of witnesses or statements given by witnesses to the commission? Can you recall that? How many such incidents like that occurred?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I don't know how many, I remember that the director Mitevski from time to time, every other day, or I can't remember how regularly when we met, apart from the other ongoing working activities that we discussed, the information that we exchanged he would also inform me about certain reports or telegrams arriving from the police stations, official material, official reports ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, I need to interrupt you for a minute. Can you please turn to paragraph 8 of that statement that you gave to my office in December 2004? I want to go over something with you. Do you see paragraph 8, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 says this: "I never saw any witness or suspect statements taken by the commission members; neither did I see any other evidence that the commission would have gathered." Does this refresh your memory now as to how often you were shown statements of people who were interviewed or notes of interviews, relating to events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: This is an abbreviated version of the answer and it should have been better to have the question in the exact form, how it was asked. First I haven't read maybe all the materials due to the simple reason that I had complete faith in the director Mitevski that he has seen a document or minutes from the meeting of the committee, I would like to clarify that no minutes were made during the meetings of the committee, so this is the spirit in which this statement was given, this paragraph, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone or to speak up a bit. We can't hear him clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you're asked to move a bit closer to the microphone and speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall -- I think I will move on. Do you recall whether during the work of the committee you received any information at all about the events in Ljuboten in August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: No specific information that something has really happened. Meaning that the rules or the regulations were violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, do you recall whether Zivko Petrovski, the other member of the commission, had an important role to play in the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I already mentioned I didn't want to meet Zivko too much, neither then nor now and therefore I would stress once again, I left at least my part to be shared with director Mitevski and under my competences everything that is a violation of the criminal code that is the prosecution, the prosecution ex officio is under the criminal police which was headed by Mr. Zivko Petrovski, while the uniformed police which I headed was then and now is in charge of maintaining law and order and/or to re-establish law and order if the law and order was in any way disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we move briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, do you recall whether Goran -- well, let me step back for a minute? What role did Goran Mitevski play in the commission; can you recall?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: With the very fact that he was appointed a head of the commission speaks enough, that the most part of the activities and the organiser of the activities was for him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, do you recall whether you ever suggested that additional investigations be carried out with respect to the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I understood the question well. I know that we insisted, especially me and Goran Mitevski and the Minister Boskoski, when we used to meet to make all possible efforts and make an on-site inspection in the village. Unfortunately, while I held that position that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, do you recall whether you ever suggested that the committee should interview persons from the Albanian side; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I think that I might have stated something like that but that was not a hearing that I heard, but the Ministry of Interior published an announcement whereby they called upon all the citizens if they have any comments or complaints about the work of the police to report on that and the minister gave the task on that matter. I don't know whether that was in writing or verbally to establish a task force that would meet with these citizens, but no one came up to complain or to state something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you take a look, please, of paragraph 9 of your statement, General? Do you see paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 says this: "I several times suggested, for example, that an on-scene investigation should be conducted and that we should interview witnesses from the Albanian side. I was trying to remain professional at all times toward all of our personnel no matter what nationality they were. At one of the meetings with the Minister Boskoski, I was ironically reprimanded by him, in terms that was too concerned with the Albanians, because I stated that cases such as the beating of a fellow police officer by the members of the Lions Special Forces just because he was of Albanian nationality should not be tolerated." General, does this accord with your recollection as to your efforts to suggest that certain additional investigations should be made?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I think this is taken out of the context from a simple reason that when I gave that statement, I think that I mentioned that but I didn't see it here, I don't see it here. There was some cases -- there was say a case when Albanian police officer was a participant in some incident, but the comment of the minister was not such as it is mentioned here. That's why I say it was taken out of context because I was born in a completely different area of Macedonia, unlike the minister who was born and he was raised together with the Albanians, and his reprimand was in the sense that I could not be worried about the Albanians as much as he could, because he had a lot of friends since childhood who were Albanian. My statement was given in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Do you know whether the commission that you belonged to ever interviewed any ethnic Albanian resident of Ljuboten; can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: The members of the committee, at least in my presence, did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall whether the committee looked into allegations of mistreatment by police officers towards ethnic Albanian detainees that took place at different police stations, different check-points in the Ljuboten-Skopje area? Did the committee investigate those allegations?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Not only as a member of the commission but as a head of the department for the police ex officio, I insisted that my subordinates who are in charge of the police in Skopje, in the city of Skopje, if-- if they have any information, to present that information. But no one came up with such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. General Galevski, do you know whether any active or reserve police officer was disciplined, punished or prosecuted for the alleged misconduct that occurred in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I think that there was no disciplinary proceeding at that moment because no report was filed against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how about since that moment, are aware of any other disciplinary proceedings since that time, since August/September 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I could not remember, because at that time the events took place so fast that I was -- that I'm not able to remember whether any disciplinary action has been initiated for this, and I could also not confirm for any other events in respect to the working discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, do you recall whether the commission that was established on the 13th of August, 2001 eventually produced a report?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like you to please turn to what is tab 2 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter number 259.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you please take a look at the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, once again we are often working with copies of copies of copies, and so the date on the copies that are in front of you is difficult to read. With the court usher's assistance I would like to show General Galevski the first page from the original copy that the Office of the Prosecutor received of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, can you take a look at this copy, please, just for a minute. You see that it says: "Republic of Macedonia, Ministry of the Interior, number 10-32424," and then there's a date. Can you see that that date is 4/9/2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, 40S [as interpreted], this looks like a nine, but I could not confirm it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: But at first glance it looks like it is 4th of 9th [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And perhaps if the usher could take that copy back. If we could have it back, please. This is a report, you'll see, submitted to the Ministry of the Interior. The subject is an examination of the circumstances and an analysis of the activities undertaken by the Security Forces for the Ministry of the Interior to repulse armed attacks by terrorist groups on 12 August 2001, village of Ljuboten-Skopje. And then it says: "Submitted by the commission formed by resolution number 07-581/01 on 13 August 2001. General, can you turn to the very last page, please. General, do you see on the very last page we see the name Goran Mitevski, director for the bureau of public security, president of the commission and then a signature. Is that Goran Mitevski's signature?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then we see below to the left, General Risto Galevski, head of the police department, member of the commission. Is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the right side we see Zivko Petrovski, director of the crime police department, member of the commission, and his signature.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I do not know whether that is his signature, but it is correct that it writes here Zivko Petrovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If you could turn back to the first page, please. And in the middle of the first page there's a paragraph beginning: "The commission, made up of Goran Mitevski." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "The commission, made up of Goran Mitevski, director of the bureau for public security in the Ministry for Internal Affairs, in his capacity as president of the commission," and then it refers to you and to Zivko Petrovski. It says: "Acting pursuant to the resolution of the 13th of August, 2001, began immediately to secure the entire written documentation available from the relevant services of the ministry relating to the activities of the Security Forces 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje and, accordingly, these authorities held a discussion with additional members of the ministry who had taken active part in the events of this case." In the next paragraph, which begins on the top of page 2 of the Macedonian version, we see that a comprehensive review of the chronology of the events was carried out with a professional review of the regulative stability of this type of activity, on the basis of which the commission affirms the following. And then we see a series of paragraphs that provides more or less a chronology of certain events that occurred in and around Ljuboten village. Do you see that on page 2 in the Macedonian version, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then turning on to page 3 of the Macedonian version, in the middle of page 3 of the Macedonian version at the bottom of page 2 of the English version, there's a paragraph that says this: "In light of the reaction which the police and armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia were forced to take, the intensity of the actions taken by the armed defence corresponded or was proportional to the attacks of the terrorist groups. In addition, the incontrovertible fact must be considered that, although above all else the members of the security are people expected to be professionals with specific accountable legal powers, in such situations," I'm continuing on the tap of page 3 in the English version. "In such situation, the reality cannot be ignored that in these circumstances there's both the human factor and a natural reaction to survive in conditions where in fact his life has been placed into real danger. And it is precisely this factor which, in the actions and the activities carried out in the village of Ljuboten caused, in a negligible number of individual events, within tolerable limits, the established equilibrium of attack/defence to be destroyed." Do you see what I've read there, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: I wasn't able to really follow it. I lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then I'd like the usher's assistance again, please, to go to the middle of page 3. I was reading from a paragraph beginning: "In light of the reaction which the police and Armed Forces of the Republic of Macedonia were forced to take." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you able to follow me --

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, now it is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And you see at the end of that paragraph it says, "In a negligible number of individual events within tolerable limits the established equilibrium of attack-defence to be destroyed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn now, General, to what is page 5, the fifth page in the Macedonian version, please. And towards the bottom of page 4 in the English version, General, on page 5 in the Macedonian version there's a paragraph that begins thus: "Bearing in mind the validity of the facts and data presented."
